guide.text: A short guideHow Utah legislation worksA reading is a procedural stage, not automatically a vote. A vote to advance a bill is not a vote on final passage.The usual orderDraft: a request becomes written legislation; a request alone is not an introduced bill.First reading: the clerk reads the bill number and short title to introduce it. It is referred for review.Committee: members consider testimony, proposed changes, and what to recommend.Second reading: the chamber handles advancement under its own rules.Third reading: the chamber considers the bill for final passage.Other chamber: the bill goes through readings and consideration there too. Both chambers must agree on the same text.Governor and effective date: a bill may be signed, vetoed, or become law without signature. Its effective date determines when provisions operate.The Constitution normally requires three title readings in each chamber; two-thirds of that chamber may suspend the requirement. Special procedures and exceptions can change the sequence.Readings: what each stage meansFirst: introduction by number and short title. A recorded first-reading action does not itself tell you that anyone voted for the bill.House second reading: the House considers the committee report and advancement to the third-reading or consent calendar. This is separate from final passage.Senate second reading: debate is followed by a roll-call vote on whether the bill should be read a third time. That is an advancement vote.Third: after the title reading and debate, the chamber takes its final-passage vote under the ordinary process.Read the action: “3rd reading” and “passed 3rd reading” describe different events. A reading entry alone does not prove passage.Votes: check the question being decidedVoice vote: members respond aloud together. The announced result is not an individual voting record.Recorded vote: an electronic or roll-call vote identifies individual votes. Some procedural questions also receive recorded votes.Committee decision: a recommendation, amendment, hold, or other committee motion is not passage by the full chamber.Procedural vote: may decide advancement, scheduling, debate, or a change to the text.Final passage: the Constitution requires yeas and nays entered in the chamber journal. The House uses an electronic or roll-call vote; the Senate uses a roll call.A legislator may vote to advance a bill and later vote against final passage. These answer different questions. Do not infer a final-passage position or motive from an earlier vote.Sponsors: three different rolesChief sponsor: the legislator who approves the request for numbering, subject to the rules for a sponsorship change.Opposite-chamber floor sponsor: the member designated by the chief sponsor to sponsor the bill in the other chamber.Cosponsors: additional legislators whose names are formally added as sponsors; names can also be removed under the rules.Sponsorship and voting are separate records. A sponsor label is not an individual roll-call result.Changes, pauses, and the other chamberAn amendment changes language; a substitute replaces a version. Compare the actual text.“Boxcar” commonly describes a bill whose substantial content arrives later. This prototype does not assign that label or infer intent.A held or circled bill pauses; that does not necessarily mean it failed. A bill may also be withdrawn or fail to advance before adjournment.If the other chamber changes the bill, further agreement is needed. Passage in one chamber alone does not make it law.Follow or participateInterim committees study issues between sessions and may recommend legislation.Read the selected version and check the official meeting agenda for public-comment instructions.Find your legislators  · Official participation FAQ Official sourcesChecked October 20, 2026 against the current published Constitution and rules. Recheck when session rules change.Utah Constitution, Article VI §22 : readings and final-passage votes.House Rules : HR4-4-101, HR4-4-201, HR4-7-201; HR3-2-403–404.Senate Rules : SR4-4-201, SR4-4-301–302, SR4-7-101 and SR4-7-201–202.Joint Rules : JR4-3-101 (introduction), JR4-2-103 (sponsorship), JR1-3-102 (journals).Official bill-to-law guide : governor and effective dates.

sources.text: Sources & methodologyBuilt on the official recordUtahBug is an independent, nonpartisan legislative-information application. Its expanded catalog contains real official 2026 measures and separately labeled public 2027 requests. Four examples retain detailed analysis. No fictional bills are presented as real, and no live coverage is claimed.What is connected?Saved official JSON records supply sponsors, actions, vote totals, committees, and document links. Official bill XML supplies statutory text. Source URLs, retrieval timestamps, and SHA-256 checksums are preserved.Catalog source manifest (opens in a new tab) · Analysis source manifest (opens in a new tab) · Download analyzed example dataset (opens in a new tab) · Official data download tool Snapshot retrieved Oct 21, 2026. 2027 bills and requests have a guarded daily refresh using official index change timestamps. The 2026 historical catalog is retained unchanged. Counts describe completeness against the retrieved index, not unpublished records. The 2027 roster is not established here. The separate Calendar has saved official scheduling information and a guarded daily refresh.What the comparisons mean“Law before proposal” reconstructs a historical baseline from the bill’s addition/deletion markup. It is not an independent historical-Code verification or a statement of current law. “Resulting text” applies the selected proposal only. Other bills, court decisions, and later amendments are not consolidated.Cross-version comparisons use proposed section text, including effective-date provisions, and normalize layout whitespace. They exclude headings, sponsor blocks, and formatting. Read the source document when precision matters.Source document dates and action dates have no explicit time zone. We do not treat retrieval dates as publication dates or calculate public-review intervals from these fields.Editorial safeguardsAI-assisted summaries identify the version used and were checked against its text during development. Independent human editorial review is pending. No paid AI service is required to build or run the site. Topic labels are editorial categories.Future automated updates must flag changed source hashes for summary re-review. Boxcar detection, substantive-change counts, resolution of remaining voting gaps, current-Code consolidation, and verified publication intervals remain future work.AccessibilityThe interface targets WCAG 2.2 AA with semantic headings, labeled native controls, visible keyboard focus, text labels for status and edits, and mobile reflow. Automated checks support development; they do not establish full conformance. Manual assistive-technology testing remains necessary.
